::: {#exm-population-mean-auto}
#### The expected fuel economy of a randomly chosen car is the average over all the cars

```{r}
#| include: false
# The Python tab in this example is the page's first Python chunk,
# so declare pandas here, and compute the counts the prose quotes
# before the code tabs run.
python_packages <- c("numpy", "pandas")
reticulate::py_require(python_packages)
auto_cars <- readr::read_csv("data/auto.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_cars <- nrow(auto_cars)
n_values <- dplyr::n_distinct(auto_cars$mpg)
```

Take the `{r} n_cars` cars in the Auto data
[described on the limit theorems page](limit-theorems.qmd#exm-clt-auto)
as the whole population.
Both code tabs in this example read this site's copy, [`data/auto.csv`](data/auto.csv).
Choose one car [at random](probability-basics.qmd#def-random-choice),
and let $Y$ be its fuel economy (`mpg`, in miles per gallon).

Many cars share a value:
the `{r} n_cars` cars have only `{r} n_values` distinct `mpg` values.
So @prp-mean-expectation does not apply,
because it needs distinct numbers,
but @prp-population-mean-expectation does.
The code tabs compute $\E{Y}$ in two ways.
The first follows the [definition](#def-expectation):
it takes the [sum](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-sums.html#def-summation) of each distinct value
times the [fraction](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-sums.html#def-fraction) of cars with that value.
The second takes the plain [average](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-vectors.html#def-mean) of `mpg` over all the cars.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Python

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
import pandas as pd

auto = pd.read_csv("data/auto.csv")

pmf = auto["mpg"].value_counts(normalize=True)
expectation_from_pmf = (pmf.index * pmf).sum()
population_average = auto["mpg"].mean()

print(f"E(Y) from the PMF:  {expectation_from_pmf:.4f}")
print(f"population average: {population_average:.4f}")
```

#### R

```{r}
#| label: population-mean-auto-r
#| code-fold: false
auto <- readr::read_csv("data/auto.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

pmf <- auto |>
  dplyr::count(mpg) |>
  dplyr::mutate(prob = n / nrow(auto))

expectation_from_pmf <- sum(pmf$mpg * pmf$prob)
population_average <- mean(auto$mpg)

c(
  "E(Y) from the PMF" = expectation_from_pmf,
  "population average" = population_average
)
```

:::

```{r}
#| include: false
# The claims the prose makes: both languages agree, values repeat,
# and the two computations of E(Y) match.
stopifnot(
  abs(expectation_from_pmf - reticulate::py$expectation_from_pmf) < 1e-9,
  abs(population_average - reticulate::py$population_average) < 1e-9,
  n_values < n_cars,
  abs(expectation_from_pmf - population_average) < 1e-9
)
```

Both computations give
$\E{Y} =$ `{r} sprintf("%.2f", population_average)` miles per gallon.
So the [expectation](#def-expectation) of the `mpg` of one car
[chosen at random](probability-basics.qmd#def-random-choice)
is the [population mean](#def-expectation) `mpg` of all `{r} n_cars` cars.
Suppose that you instead draw many cars [at random](probability-basics.qmd#def-random-choice), with replacement.
Then the [average](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-vectors.html#def-mean) of their `mpg` values settles near this number,
as [the remark on long-run averages](limit-theorems.qmd#rem-expectation-long-run-average) explains.

<!-- no-figure: the example compares two computations of one number -->

:::
